lessons.title: Covenants, Collateral and Credit Ratings: The Strings Attached to Debt

children.text: A loan agreement runs to forty pages. The interest rate is on page one, and it is the only thing most borrowers read carefully. The parts that decide whether the loan becomes dangerous sit between pages twelve and thirty, in the sections nobody discusses at sanction and everybody discusses in a bad quarter.
This lesson covers the three of them: the conditions you must keep meeting, the assets the lender can take, and the rating that sets your price.

body.text: You can pay every rupee of interest on time and still be in default. Covenants make the loan conditional on how the business performs, not just on whether you paid.

children.text: Covenants: The Conditions You Keep Meeting
A
covenant
is a promise about the future, tested repeatedly through the life of the loan. Indian lenders use three kinds.

markDefs.definition: A condition written into a loan agreement that the borrower must keep meeting. Breaching one is a default even if every rupee of interest has been paid on time.

cells: Keeping defined ratios within agreed limits, tested quarterly or annually
Debt to EBITDA below 3.5x, interest coverage above 2x, DSCR above 1.25x, current ratio above 1.33x
File audited accounts within a set period, submit monthly stock statements, keep assets insured, maintain the account as the primary banker
Things you must not do without consent
Take on new borrowing, create a second charge, sell fixed assets, pay dividends above a limit, change shareholding or management, invest in group companies

body.text: The negative covenant list is where borrowers get trapped. A clause requiring lender consent before any new borrowing means your existing bank effectively controls your access to every other lender. Negotiate a threshold, for example borrowings up to ₹5 crore permitted without consent, rather than accepting a blanket prohibition.

children.text: The Three Ratios You Will Be Tested On
Most Indian financial covenants reduce to variations of three calculations. Learn these three and you can read almost any sanction letter.

body.caption: How many times over operating profit covers the interest bill
Whether the business generates enough cash to service debt, including repayment
Roughly, how many years of operating profit it would take to repay the debt

children.text: Note the difference between the first two. The
interest coverage ratio
asks only whether interest is comfortable. The
debt service coverage ratio
includes principal repayment, which is why a company can show healthy interest coverage and still fail its DSCR test.

markDefs.definition: Operating profit divided by interest cost. It shows how many times over the company can pay its interest bill.
Cash available for debt service divided by the interest and principal due in the same period. Below 1 means the business is not generating enough to pay its debt.

body.title: Test the DSCR
body.prompt: A company generates ₹9 crore of cash available for debt service this year. It owes ₹4 crore of interest and ₹3 crore of principal repayment in the same year. What is its DSCR? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: ₹9 crore divided by ₹7 crore of total debt service is 1.29x. Against a typical covenant of 1.25x this just passes. Note how thin that is: a 4% fall in cash flow, or one delayed customer payment, breaches it.

body.title: The covenant that breaks
body.prompt: A company has ₹120 crore of total borrowings and a covenant requiring debt to EBITDA below 3.5x. EBITDA falls to ₹28 crore. What is the ratio now? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹120 crore divided by ₹28 crore is 4.29x, comfortably above the 3.5x limit. Nothing about the borrowing changed. The covenant broke because profit fell, which is precisely when a company least wants its lender to gain new rights over it.

body.title: Debt to EBITDA against the covenant limit (x)

stats.label: FY25
stats.context: Tightening, worth flagging to the board

body.text: Read the chart from the left, not the right. The FY25 number is the useful one: still compliant, but clearly heading the wrong way. A finance team that calls the bank at that point negotiates from a position of competence. One that waits until FY26 is negotiating after a default.

children.text: What Actually Happens When a Covenant Breaks
A covenant breach without a missed payment is often called a technical default. It is not a minor thing, but it is not the same as failing to pay.

columns.label: Technical default (covenant breach)
points: A ratio or condition is missed, payments are current
There is usually a cure period to fix it
The lender may grant a waiver, often for a fee
Common outcomes: higher interest, tighter conditions, more reporting
The lender gains the right to recall, but usually does not use it immediately

columns.label: Payment default
points: Interest or principal has not been paid on the due date
Penal interest applies from day one
The account moves towards special mention and then non-performing classification
Enforcement of security becomes a live option
Credit rating and future access to debt are damaged for years

children.text: The dangerous clause in either case is
cross-default

. If you breach a covenant with one lender, every other loan agreement carrying a cross-default clause can be declared in default too, even though those lenders have been paid in full. One problem becomes every problem on the same day.

markDefs.definition: A clause stating that a default under any other loan agreement is automatically a default under this one, even if this lender has been paid in full.

body.title: What should the CFO do first?
body.question: A company realises in the second month of a quarter that its debt to EBITDA will breach the covenant when quarterly results are filed six weeks from now. Payments are all current. What is the best first action?
options: Say nothing and hope the lender does not check
Approach the lender proactively with the numbers and a plan, and ask for a waiver or a reset of the covenant
Repay the loan immediately using working capital funds
Draw down every available limit before the breach is reported
body.explanation: Lenders discover breaches. They almost always respond better to a borrower who brings the problem early with a credible plan than to one who is found out at filing. Drawing down every limit before a known breach is the worst option: it looks like bad faith and can itself trigger clauses in the agreement.

body.title: How enforcement actually works in India

children.text: If a borrower stops paying, a secured lender does not have to start a court case from scratch. Under the SARFAESI Act, 2002, a secured creditor can issue a demand notice and, if the borrower still does not pay, take possession of and sell the secured assets, subject to the procedure and timelines in the Act.

Separately, an unresolved default of the prescribed threshold can be taken to the National Company Law Tribunal under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, where control of the company passes to a resolution professional and the promoters lose the ability to run it. That route is covered in the next lesson.

For a borrower, the sequence matters: covenant breach gives the lender rights, payment default gives it remedies, and sustained default hands the company itself to a process the promoters do not control.
Collateral: How Much Cover a Lender Wants
Lenders do not lend rupee for rupee against asset value. They apply a margin, or haircut, so that the security remains worth more than the loan even if values fall or recovery is slow. The measure is
security cover

markDefs.definition: The value of the charged assets divided by the loan outstanding. Lenders require a cushion so they can recover even if asset values fall.

body.caption: A cover of 1.25x means ₹1.25 of assets charged for every ₹1 borrowed

body.title: Check the cover
body.prompt: A bank has lent ₹10 crore against assets it values at ₹14 crore. What is the security cover? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹14 crore divided by ₹10 crore is 1.4x. If the sanction required a minimum of 1.25x, there is headroom. If asset values fell 15%, cover would drop to about 1.19x and the bank could ask for additional security, which is a covenant in its own right.

children.text: In the bond market the equivalent requirement is set by regulation rather than negotiation. SEBI requires issuers of listed secured debt securities to maintain security cover of at least 100% of the principal, and listed entities file a security cover certificate, with book values certified by the statutory auditor, on a quarterly basis.

body.text: Asset value is the lender's valuation, not yours. Specialised machinery may be worth a great deal to your production line and very little at a distress sale, which is exactly the value a lender is underwriting. Expect deep haircuts on anything with a thin resale market.

children.text: Credit Ratings: The Price Tag on Your Balance Sheet
For any company borrowing from the bond market, and increasingly for large bank facilities, a rating from CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings is what sets the cost of money.

body.caption: The Indian long-term rating scale, simplified

cells: Cheapest borrowing available to a corporate
Still very cheap, widely held by institutions
Moderate safety, the lowest investment grade
Effectively shut out of the bond market

children.text: Anything from AAA down to BBB minus is
investment grade

, and that boundary matters enormously: many regulated investors are restricted from holding anything below it. A single-notch downgrade from BBB minus to BB plus can remove most of your potential buyers at once. Short-term instruments such as commercial paper use a separate scale, from A1 plus down to A4, and then D.

markDefs.definition: Ratings from AAA down to BBB minus, which regulated investors such as insurers and pension funds are generally permitted to hold.

body.label: How fast a rating can collapse
body.value: IL&FS went from AAA to D in weeks in 2018
body.context: ICRA cut IL&FS from AAA to AA plus in August 2018, then multiple notches to BB in early September, and to D on 17 September 2018 after the company failed to service commercial paper. SEBI later penalised rating agencies in connection with the episode. For a borrower the lesson is blunt: a rating reflects a view that can change far faster than a business can refinance, so never build a funding plan that assumes your rating is stable.

children.text: Rating-linked pricing.
Many Indian loan and bond documents include a step-up clause: a downgrade automatically raises your coupon or spread.
Rating triggers as covenants.
Some agreements treat a downgrade below a stated level as an event of default in itself.
Ratings cut both ways.
An upgrade is a genuine negotiating tool. Take it to your bankers and ask for the spread to be reduced.

body.title: The line that matters
body.textWithBlank: On the Indian long-term rating scale, the lowest investment grade rating is ___ minus, and anything below it is sub-investment grade.
body.explanation: BBB minus is the boundary. Below it, many insurers, pension funds and debt mutual funds either cannot invest or will not, which is why a single notch at that point changes the cost of money so sharply.

body.title: Price the downgrade
body.question: A company rated AA has ₹400 crore of bonds outstanding with a step-up clause adding 75 basis points on a downgrade to A. The downgrade happens. What is the annual increase in interest cost?
options: Nothing, because the bonds were already issued
body.explanation: 75 basis points is 0.75%. On ₹400 crore that is ₹3 crore a year. Step-up clauses mean a downgrade raises the cost of debt you have already raised, at exactly the moment the business is under pressure. This is why treasury teams monitor rating sensitivities, not just interest rates.

body.label: CRISIL Ratings
body.description: Search any rated Indian company and read its rating rationale. These documents state plainly what the agency thinks of the business, its covenants and its refinancing risk, and they are free to read.

body.title: The waiver negotiation
body.scenario: You are the finance controller of a mid-size Nashik packaging company. A ₹45 crore term loan carries covenants requiring debt to EBITDA below 3.5x, DSCR above 1.25x and no fresh borrowing without lender consent. A large customer has delayed payments and a raw material price spike has hit margins. Your projections show debt to EBITDA at about 4.3x at the March year end, with DSCR around 1.10x. Payments are current and cash flow is expected to recover by the second quarter of the next financial year.
body.prompt: How would you prepare for and run the conversation with the lender?
body.modelAnswer:
Before the meeting:
1. Quantify precisely. Show the breach, its causes split between the customer delay and the input cost spike, and how much of each is temporary. Vague reassurance is what makes lenders nervous.
2. Build a monthly cash flow to the expected recovery, with a downside case. Bring both, and be the one who raises the downside first.
3. Check every other loan agreement for cross-default clauses. If they exist, a breach here is a breach everywhere, and you need to approach those lenders in the same week rather than being discovered.
4. Identify what you can offer: promoter infusion, a temporary reduction in capex, faster collection on other receivables, additional security, or a partial prepayment from a specific inflow.

What to ask for:
5. A waiver for the testing date, in writing, not a verbal comfort. Expect a fee and a possible spread increase, and know in advance what you are willing to pay.
6. Better still, a reset: covenants recalibrated to a realistic trajectory for the next four quarters, so you are not returning for a waiver every quarter.
7. Relief on the specific covenant that is genuinely at risk, rather than a broad renegotiation that invites the bank to reopen everything.

What to avoid:
8. Do not draw down remaining limits just before the breach is reported.
9. Do not let the auditor's report be the lender's first information. A covenant breach at year end raises questions about classification and disclosure, and the finance team should have briefed the lender and the audit committee well before that.
10. Do not agree to a personal guarantee as the reflex price of a waiver without testing whether additional security or a higher spread would satisfy the lender instead.

The underlying point: a technical default is a negotiation. It becomes a crisis only when the borrower handles it late or dishonestly.

body.title: Covenant hygiene for any borrowing company
steps: List every financial covenant, its exact definition and its testing date
Recalculate each ratio monthly, not at year end, using the lender's definition rather than your own
Track headroom as a percentage, so you can see a breach coming two quarters out
Know which agreements contain cross-default clauses
Know what consents are needed before new borrowing, asset sales or dividends
Diarise every reporting obligation: stock statements, audited accounts, insurance renewals
Watch your credit rating and any step-up or rating trigger clauses tied to it

cards.definition: A condition in a loan agreement that must keep being met. Breach is a default even if payments are current.
Cash available for debt service divided by interest plus principal due.
Total borrowings divided by operating profit before depreciation.
A covenant breach with payments current. Usually curable or waivable, often at a price.
A default under one agreement triggering default under others.
Value of charged assets divided by loan outstanding. SEBI requires at least 100% for listed secured debt.
AAA down to BBB minus. Below that, most regulated investors step away.

points: Covenants make a loan conditional on performance. You can be in default with every payment made on time.
Three ratios cover most Indian covenants: interest coverage, DSCR and debt to EBITDA.
DSCR includes principal repayment, so it fails earlier than interest coverage.
A covenant breaks when profit falls, not when borrowing rises, which is why breaches cluster in bad quarters.
Cross-default clauses turn one lender's problem into every lender's problem on the same day.
Lenders require security cover above 1x, and SEBI mandates at least 100% cover for listed secured debt securities.
Ratings set the price of debt and can collapse quickly, as IL&FS showed in 2018. Step-up clauses make a downgrade expensive immediately.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. Covenant levels, security cover requirements and rating scales are described in general terms and vary by lender, instrument and date. Enforcement processes are summarised, not stated exhaustively. Take professional advice on any actual loan agreement or covenant breach.
